extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset of narrative passages for word prediction requiring broad discourse context understanding. Each passage consists of a context (average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence where the last word must be predicted. Human subjects can guess the target word when exposed to the whole passage, but not when seeing only the last sentence.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.citeAs: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1525–1534, Berlin, Germany, August 7-12, 2016.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were extracted from the Book Corpus containing unpublished novels. A random sample of passages were evaluated by human subjects through CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject guessed based on the whole passage; (3) if also correct, more subjects tried to guess based on target sentence only until the word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses were reached.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Book Corpus containing unpublished novels. The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Passages were filtered using a combination of four language models (a pre-trained RNN, a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded. The vocabulary of the models was restricted to the 60K most frequent words in the training set (covering 95% of the target words in the development set).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Passages were filtered using four language models (pre-trained RNN, 4-gram model, RNN, and feed-forward model trained on Book Corpus). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any language model was excluded. Duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material with a stop word list was performed on the corpus.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects guessed target words through a three-step crowdsourcing process. Step 1: one subject guessed based on whole passage. Step 2: if correct, second subject guessed based on whole passage. Step 3: if also correct, subjects tried to guess based on target sentence only (3 guesses per sentence allowed) until word was guessed or 10 unsuccessful guesses reached. Only passages where no subject guessed the word from sentence context alone were included.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses. Perfect-match approach was used rather than accepting plausible or synonymous continuations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Variable: 2 subjects for whole passage guessing (steps 1-2), and up to 10 subjects for sentence-only guessing (step 3)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models used for filtering: pre-trained RNN (Mikolov et al., 2011), 4-gram model, RNN, and feed-forward model trained on Book Corpus
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Development set and training corpus available for download. Test set to be made available at time of planned public competition.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset shows bias toward proper nouns (48% of target words), which are hugely over-represented compared to the input data. Common nouns constitute 37% and verbs only 7.7%. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context. The dataset contains quoted direct speech significantly more often than input items overall (71% vs 61%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to cases where the target word can be exactly matched by human subjects. Alternative plausible or synonymous continuations were not included due to practical and methodological challenges in determining which answers fit well. The dataset is designed to be challenging for language models by filtering out easier cases. Standard language models are bound to fail by design due to the filtering process.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing: The dataset is designed as a challenging test set to evaluate computational models for text understanding through word prediction requiring broad discourse context. Training: Models should be trained on raw text from the training partition (2662 novels, 200M+ words). Development: The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of LAMBADA passages.

name.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.

description.evidence: LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To reduce time and cost of dataset collection, we filtered out passages that are relatively easy for standard language models, since such cases are likely to be guessable based on local context alone. We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model; see SM for details, and note that these are different from the models we evaluated on LAMBADA as described in Section 4 below). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: For a given passage, 1. one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage (comprising the context and the target sentence); if the guess was right, 2. a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. The subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence, to maximize the chances of catching cases where the target words were guessable from the sentence alone.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%). In fact, proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input... More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context, while in the input data that was the case for less than 15% of the passages... the LAMBADA items contain (quoted) direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample)

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: An altemative to this perfect-match approach would have been to include passages where broad-context subjects provided other plausible or synonymous continuations. However, it is very challenging, both practically and methodologically, to determine which answers other than the original fit the passage well... We recognize, of course, that the evaluation we performed is very preliminary, and it must only be taken as a proof-of-concept study of the difficulty of LAMBADA... We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text... The training data for language models to be tested on LAMBADA include the full text of 2,662 novels (disjoint from those in dev+test), comprising 203 million words... The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages.
